entry: Romantic or sexual relationship between people of the same sex or gender. Some same-sex couples have children, biological or non-biological, such as adoptive or foster children, and raise them with their partner. [[Same-sex marriage]] is the institutionalized recognition of such relationships; civil unions exist in some countries where it does not. The phrase *same-gender relationship* is now used interchangeably with *same-sex relationship*. Earlier usage spoke of homosexual, gay or lesbian relationships, a usage described as erasing bisexual and transgender people. The lives of many historical figures, including [[Socrates]], [[Alexander the Great]], [[Edward II]] and [[Michelangelo]], are believed to have included same-sex love, though whether terms such as gay or bisexual apply to them is disputed. Same-sex love appears in the work of Persian writers such as [[Omar Khayyam]], and in Japanese *shudo* literature and shunga art.

Gaelic festival on 1 November marking the end of the harvest season and the beginning of winter. Believed to have Celtic pagan origins, it is mentioned in Irish literature from the 9th century, when gatherings and feasts were held and ancient burial mounds, seen as portals to the Otherworld, were open. In the 9th century the Western Church made 1 November All Saints' Day, and Samhain is believed to have influenced, and been influenced by, the modern [[Halloween]]. Since the late 20th century, Celtic neopagans and [[Wicca|Wiccans]] have observed it as a religious holiday.

American singer, actor, comedian and dancer known as "Mr. Entertainment." He began in vaudeville at age two with the Will Mastin Trio, and his career breakthrough came in 1951. In 1954 he became the first Black entertainer to headline a show in [[Las Vegas]]. As a member of the Rat Pack he performed with [[Frank Sinatra]] and [[Dean Martin]]. His 1955 debut album topped the Billboard pop albums chart. In 1954 he lost his left eye in a car accident, and in 1960 he converted to Judaism. He died of lung cancer in 1990, in debt to the Internal Revenue Service.

American former mobster who became a government witness. Gravano rose to underboss of the Gambino crime family in [[New York City]] and confessed to involvement in at least 19 murders. In 1991 he agreed to testify against boss [[John Gotti]] after Gotti's remarks about him were captured on a wiretap. Gotti received a life sentence without parole in 1992. Gravano's own 1994 sentence of five years amounted to less than one year after credit for time served. In 2002 he was sentenced to 20 years in New York on drug charges, and he was released in September 2017.

Island country in Polynesia, Oceania, in the [[Pacific Ocean|South Pacific Ocean]] (pop., 2024: 208,853). Its two main islands are Savai'i and Upolu, with several smaller ones; the capital and largest city is Apia. The Lapita people settled the islands around 3,500 years ago. The country became a colony of the [[German Empire]] in 1899, known as German Samoa. New Zealand troops occupied it in August 1914, at the start of [[World War I]], and New Zealand administered it under a [[League of Nations]] mandate from 1920, as Western Samoa. It became a [[United Nations]] trust territory in 1946 and gained independence on 1 January 1962. The name was changed back to Samoa in 1997. Samoa is a unitary parliamentary democracy and a member of the [[Commonwealth of Nations]]; it was admitted to the United Nations in 1976. Its land area is 2,831 sq km.

Mozambican politician and revolutionary, first president of Mozambique from independence in 1975. Born in Gaza Province to a farming family, he trained as a nurse in Lourenço Marques (now [[Maputo]]) before leaving the country to join the nationalist movement FRELIMO in [[Dar es Salaam]]. He rose to command its guerrillas in the independence war and then the army. As president he established a one-party state on the principles of [[Marxism–Leninism]], nationalized key sectors of the economy and pursued rural collectivization and literacy campaigns. A civil war against the RENAMO rebels, who received support from [[South Africa]] and Rhodesia, followed. Machel died when a Tupolev Tu-134 crashed near Mbuzini, South Africa, killing 34 people. A South African inquiry blamed Soviet pilot error; Mozambican and Soviet investigations alleged a false navigational beacon.

Selection of a subset of individuals from a [[Statistical population|statistical population]], used to estimate characteristics of the whole. Sampling is central to statistics, [[Survey methodology|survey methodology]] and quality assurance. It costs less and yields data faster than a [[Census]] of the entire population, which is often impossible. Samples should be representative, and statisticians aim for an unbiased group; survey weights can adjust for the design, particularly in stratified sampling. Random sampling by lots is mentioned several times in the [[Bible]]. In 1786 Pierre Simon Laplace estimated the population of France from a sample. A famous failure came in 1936, when the Literary Digest predicted a Republican win in the U.S. presidential election, because its subscription and telephone lists were heavily [[Bias|biased]] toward Republicans. Probability methods include simple random, systematic, stratified and cluster sampling.

Last of the judges of the ancient [[Israelites]] in the Book of Judges, famed for superhuman strength. As a Nazirite he slew a lion bare-handed and killed a Philistine army with a donkey's jawbone. Betrayed by his lover Delilah, who had his hair cut while he slept, he was blinded and made to grind grain for the [[Philistines]]. In the temple of Dagon he prayed for strength, pushed down its pillars and died with his enemies. Some Christians have seen him as a type of [[Jesus]]. Many scholars regard the stories as folk legend rather than reliable history.

South Korean multinational [[Conglomerate (company)|conglomerate]] and the largest *chaebol*, a family-controlled business group, headquartered in [[Seoul]]. Founded in 1938 by Lee Byung-chul as a trading company, it diversified into food processing, textiles, [[Insurance|insurance]], securities and retail. It entered electronics in the late 1960s, starting with black-and-white television sets, and construction and [[Shipbuilding|shipbuilding]] in the mid-1970s. After Lee died in 1987 the group was divided into five business groups. Its key affiliate Samsung Electronics was the world's largest information technology company by 2017 revenues, and Samsung Heavy Industries was the world's second-largest shipbuilder by 2010 revenues. Samsung ranked fifth in the world for brand value as of 2024. Its leaders have been convicted of corruption, and critics argue that state-favored industrial policies distort competition.

Series of mobile computing devices designed and marketed by Samsung Electronics since 2009. The line includes the Galaxy S series of high-end smartphones, the foldable Galaxy Z series, the mid-range Galaxy A, M and F series, the Galaxy Tab tablets and the Galaxy Watch smartwatches. The first Galaxy, launched in June 2009, was Samsung's first [[Android (operating system)|Android]]-powered device. The Galaxy S and S II were very successful and helped bring Android into the mainstream in the early 2010s. The Galaxy XR, released on 21 October 2025, is one of the first major extended-reality devices to run Android XR.

Second emperor of the [[Gupta Empire]] of ancient India. The son of Chandragupta I and the Licchavi princess Kumaradevi, he transformed the kingdom into a vast empire through military campaigns. The Allahabad Pillar inscription, a eulogy composed by his courtier Harisena, credits him with defeating nine kings of northern India and annexing their territories, and with a southern campaign against twelve kingdoms whose rulers became tributaries. At his height his direct rule extended from the Ravi River in the west to the [[Brahmaputra River]] in the east, and from the Himalayan foothills to central India. He performed the Ashvamedha sacrifice to assert his sovereignty and remained undefeated in battle. His gold coins and inscriptions suggest he was a poet and played the veena. His son [[Chandragupta II]] continued his expansionist policy. Scholars variously date his reign from c. 319 to c. 350 CE.

American statesman and Founding Father, second cousin of [[John Adams]]. A politician in colonial Massachusetts, he founded the Sons of Liberty and opposed British taxation of the colonies. His 1768 Massachusetts Circular Letter urged non-cooperation, and in 1772 he devised a committee of correspondence system that linked patriots throughout the [[Thirteen Colonies]]. He helped guide the Continental Congress in [[Philadelphia]] toward the Continental Association in 1774 and the Declaration of Independence in 1776. He was later elected governor of Massachusetts. Historians disagree on his methods: 19th-century accounts praised him, while early 20th-century accounts called him a propagandist.

Irish playwright, novelist and poet who wrote in English and French. His best-known play, *Waiting for Godot* (1953), is a tragicomedy that helped transform modern theatre. Beckett lived mostly in Paris and was a close friend of [[James Joyce]], whom he cited as a major inspiration. His later plays became increasingly austere and minimalistic, relying on repetition and self-reference. Martin Esslin called much of his work part of the "Theatre of the Absurd." During the Second World War he joined the French Resistance group Gloria SMH and was awarded the Croix de Guerre in 1945. He received the 1969 Nobel Prize in Literature. In 1961 he shared the inaugural International Prix with [[Jorge Luis Borges]]. He is buried at the Cimetière du Montparnasse, and the Samuel Beckett Bridge in [[Dublin]] is named for him.

Cameroonian football administrator and former striker, president of the Cameroonian Football Federation. He won the [[UEFA Champions League]] with [[FC Barcelona]] in 2006 and 2009, scoring in both finals, and with [[Inter Milan]] in 2010. He was African Player of the Year a record four times and is the all-time leading scorer in the history of the Africa Cup of Nations, with 18 goals. With Cameroon he won the 2000 Olympic gold medal and the Africa Cup of Nations in 2000 and 2002. He announced his retirement from international football in 2014.

Polish-born American film producer and pioneer of the American film industry. Born Szmuel Gelbfisz in [[Warsaw]], he emigrated to England and then to the United States in 1899, working in the glove business in Gloversville, New York, before entering films. In 1913 he co-founded the Jesse L. Lasky Feature Play Company with [[Cecil B. DeMille]] and others; its production of *The Squaw Man* was among the first feature films made in Hollywood. Goldwyn Pictures, formed in 1916 with the Selwyn brothers, is remembered for its "Leo the Lion" trademark. The company merged into [[Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer]] in 1924, but Goldwyn continued as an independent producer. He made literary adaptations, including *Dodsworth* (1936) and *The Best Years of Our Lives* (1946), which won the Academy Award for Best Picture. He received the Irving G. Thalberg Memorial Award in 1947.

English writer, poet and lexicographer, best known for *A Dictionary of the English Language* (1755). The dictionary, with 42,733 entries, took nine years to compile and remained pre-eminent until the [[Oxford English Dictionary]] appeared some 150 years later. Johnson also wrote the poem *London* (1738), the play *Irene* (1749) and *The Lives of the Most Eminent English Poets* (1779–1781), which combined biography and criticism. His friend James Boswell's *Life of Samuel Johnson* (1791) is regarded as a landmark of biography. A devout Anglican and committed Tory, Johnson became a celebrated conversationalist in London literary circles. He is buried in [[Westminster Abbey]].

American actor and film producer, whose films have grossed more than $27 billion worldwide, the most of any actor. His breakout role as a hitman in [[Pulp Fiction]] (1994) brought a BAFTA Award and an Academy Award nomination for Best Supporting Actor. He has collaborated with [[Quentin Tarantino]] on many films and with [[Spike Lee]] in six. He played the Jedi Mace Windu in the [[Star Wars]] prequel trilogy and Nick Fury in 11 Marvel Cinematic Universe films. He has received an Academy Honorary Award.

American serial killer who confessed to 93 murders across 19 states between 1970 and 2005. He was convicted of eight murders. The FBI's Violent Criminal Apprehension Program confirmed his involvement in at least 60, the largest number of confirmed victims for any American serial killer. Most of the murders were concentrated in [[Miami]] and [[Los Angeles]]. Little provided sketches for 26 of his victims. In 2014 he was convicted in California of three murders from the 1980s, and he died in custody. He had been raised by his grandmother in [[Ohio|Lorain, Ohio]].

American inventor and painter, co-developer of [[Morse code]]. After establishing his reputation as a portrait painter, he produced his masterpiece, *The Dying Hercules*, while in England. In middle age he contributed to a single-wire telegraph system based on European telegraphs, and he helped develop its commercial use. He co-developed Morse code in 1837 and demonstrated the telegraph publicly in 1844 with the message "What hath God wrought." He also helped found the National Academy of Design in 1825 and served as its first president. He experimented with early photography after encountering the process of [[Louis Daguerre]]. His 1835 book *Foreign Conspiracy Against the Liberties of the United States* warned of Catholic and European plots, reflecting nativist fears of cultural change.

English poet, literary critic, philosopher and theologian, a founder of the Romantic movement in England. With [[William Wordsworth]] he collaborated on *Lyrical Ballads* (1798). He wrote the poems *The Rime of the Ancient Mariner* and "Kubla Khan", and the prose work *Biographia Literaria* (1817), which distinguished fancy from imagination. He helped introduce German idealist philosophy to England. Through his interpretation of [[Immanuel Kant]]'s concept of intuition, he influenced [[Ralph Waldo Emerson]] and the beginnings of [[Transcendentalism|American transcendentalism]]. He coined phrases such as "suspension of disbelief." He was given laudanum for illness, which fostered a lifelong opium addiction. His public esteem grew after his death.

Member of the professional warrior class in pre-industrial [[Japan]], who served as retainers to the lords. Samurai trained from youth in swordsmanship, archery and horsemanship, and also studied literature, calligraphy and Confucian philosophy. The word is thought to derive from a term meaning "one who serves." Under the [[Tokugawa shogunate]], prolonged peace turned the warrior estate into a hereditary administrative class; many samurai served as officials, police and teachers while keeping stipends and the right to bear arms. A ronin was a samurai who had lost his master. After the [[Meiji Restoration]] the abolition of the domains, conscription and the removal of sword-wearing dismantled the basis of samurai status. These classes were legally recognized until 1947, and in the 1918 census former warriors known as shizoku made up 4.06% of the population.

Continental right-lateral strike-slip fault about 750 mi (1,210 km) long through [[California]], forming part of the boundary between the Pacific and North American plates. Its average slip rate is 20 to 35 mm per year. In the north it ends at the Mendocino triple junction, where three plates meet. In the south it ends near the [[Salton Sea]], where the plate boundary is rifting apart. Andrew Lawson of UC Berkeley identified the fault in 1895 and, after the 1906 San Francisco earthquake, mapped the offsets along surface ruptures to show that it had been the source.

City in the southern part of [[Texas]], United States, and the county seat of Bexar County. It is the seventh-most populous city in the United States and the second-most populous in Texas after [[Houston]], with 1.43 million residents at the 2020 census. A Spanish expedition named the site in 1691 for Saint Anthony of Padua. A Spanish mission and presidio were founded there in 1718, and it became the first chartered civil settlement in present-day Texas in 1731. It passed from the [[Spanish Empire]] to Mexico and then, after the annexation of the [[Republic of Texas]] in 1846, to the United States. Five 18th-century Spanish missions, including The Alamo, are UNESCO World Heritage sites. The city is a major military hub, home to Fort Sam Houston, and about 64% of its residents are Hispanic.

City on the Pacific coast of Southern California, next to the Mexican border and the county seat of San Diego County. It is the eighth-most populous city in the United States and the second-most populous in California, with over 1.4 million residents. Known for a mild [[Mediterranean climate]], beaches and a long association with the U.S. Navy, the city's largest sectors are military and defense, tourism, international trade, research and manufacturing. The Spanish explorer Juan Rodríguez Cabrillo claimed the bay for [[Spain]] in 1542, and the Presidio and Mission San Diego de Alcalá, founded in 1769, formed the first European settlement in what is now California. The city is the economic center of the San Diego–[[Tijuana]] region, and the San Ysidro Port of Entry there is the busiest international land border crossing outside Asia.

Metropolitan region of Northern California surrounding San Francisco Bay, anchored by Oakland, San Francisco and San Jose. Its combined statistical area has over nine million people and is the second-largest in California. It houses the global center of the technology industry and is a nexus for healthcare, education, finance and tourism. The Ohlone and Miwok peoples lived in the area long before Spanish colonization, and the 1848 gold rush brought rapid growth. A major earthquake and fire leveled much of San Francisco in 1906. It is home to [[University of California, Berkeley|UC Berkeley]] and [[Stanford University]], which helped create [[Silicon Valley]].
